title: Ramsar Sites: Why Wetlands Get a List

endcard.line: Pictures: Government of Odisha (CC BY 4.0); Nagarjun (CC BY 2.0); Haoreima (CC BY 4.0)

segments.say: Marshes, lakes, lagoons, mangroves. Wetlands clean water, soak up floods and feed millions of birds. Yet for years they were drained as wasteland.
In nineteen seventy-one, countries signed a treaty in the Iranian town of Ramsar to protect them. India joined in nineteen eighty-two.
A Ramsar site is a wetland of international importance. The country picks it, and promises to use it wisely, not to lock it away.
India's first two were Chilika Lake in Odisha and Keoladeo in Rajasthan, a bird paradise.

anim.title: The Montreux Record
items: A watch list of sites in danger
Indian sites on it: Keoladeo, Loktak
Chilika was removed in 2002 after it recovered

segments.say: Sites in trouble go on a watch list, the Montreux Record. Keoladeo and Loktak are on it. Chilika was taken off in two thousand two after it recovered.
Loktak in Manipur is famous for its floating islands, called phumdis. India's list has grown fast, to more than eighty sites.
For Prelims: Ramsar, nineteen seventy-one. India joined in eighty-two. On the Montreux Record: Keoladeo and Loktak.

sources: Ramsar Convention Secretariat (ramsar.org): Convention signed 2 February 1971 at Ramsar, Iran; 'wise use'; Montreux Record of sites with change in ecological character; India party since 1 February 1982; Chilika and Keoladeo designated 1981
Ramsar Sites Information Service, India: Keoladeo National Park and Loktak Lake on the Montreux Record; Chilika removed from the Record in 2002
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change / PIB releases on new Ramsar sites (2024–25): India's count above 80
